summary:
The ARES Project refers to a Microgravity Combustion and Habitat Fire Safety Workbench created using NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI) data provenance. The project is designed with dual modes for Engineers and for Public/Students, and the interactive platform allows users to analyze fire behaviors and risks in different space flight conditions. Users can set mission target parameters such as ambient oxygen mole fraction, total cabin pressure, forced convective airflow, and gravity fields (0g orbital, 1/6g Lunar, 3/8g Martian, and 1g Earth reference) along with fire safety principles and fuel regime in order to filter and export telemetry datasets in .CSV and .JSON formats.

This workbench helps to solve the critical problem of how fires behave in microgravity space habitats versus fires on Earth since conventional fire safety models are not sufficient due to different buoyancy and flow dynamics in space. Through translating the complex microgravity combustion data sets into an analyzable tool, Project ARES helps mission planners in creating more secure spacecrafts and space habitats while providing STEM education on space fire physics.
details:
What It Does and How It Works:

Project ARES is an interactive workbench that is based on NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion datasets. In ARES, users set up habitat boundary conditions including O2 percentage, cabin pressure, airflow, and gravity (0g, 1/6g, 3/8g, 1g) through various presets like ISS Baseline or Lunar Habitat. Through four different modules, users: (1) rate matching NASA experiments (Empirical Coverage); (2) compare hardware racks and fuel phases against each other (Experiment Diff); (3) find O2/pressure research gaps (Unknown Frontier); and (4) search indexed PSI datasets via evidence-grounded synthesis engine (Ask ARES). Filtered matrixes are exportable in .CSV and .JSON format.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

The workbench saves research time by integrating fragmented ISS rack data (MSG and CIR) and by preventing dangerous extrapolation into unexplored partial-gravity environments. The intended impact of the tool is enabling the safe design of fire prevention, detection, and extinguishing in Artemis habitats, Gateway, and Mars missions, while also bringing attention to Earth applications (like flame-retardant fabrics and mist suppression) and teaching spacefire physics to students.

Tools, Languages, and Software Used:

Project ARES is created using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript. It features custom interactive visualizations, dynamic SVG-based flame-physics graphics, evidence-grounded retrieval/synthesis engine that is indexed on NASA PSI metadata, and web deployment with Netlify. (Please update with any specific frameworks and APIs used in the project.)

Creativity and Team Considerations:

Project ARES creatively combines the hard facts of telemetry with Public/Student mode that contains dynamic flame shape graphics and “Earth benefits” sections. The gap in current scientific understanding is illustrated in a visual way. The team took into account exploration atmosphere parameters (high O2, low pressure), lack of actual 1/6g and 3/8g flight data, hardware/fuel phase mismatch, and false-alarm smoke detectors caused by dust from the lunar regolith.
